    Calculate Field-Normalized Citation Impact

    Source: R/metric-fnci.R
    sm_metric_fnci.Rd

    Computes the Field-Normalized Citation Impact (FNCI) for each work in the corpus. FNCI normalises a work's citation count by the average citation count of all works in the same field and publication year.

    Usage

    sm_metric_fnci(
  corpus,
  classification = c("openalex_concepts", "mesh", "manual"),
  min_cell = NULL,
  by_type = FALSE,
  call = rlang::caller_env()
)

    Arguments

    corpus

    An sm_corpus object.

    classification

    Character; the classification system used to assign works to fields. One of "openalex_concepts" (default), "mesh", or "manual".

    min_cell

    NULL (default) or a positive integer. When set, a baseline needs at least min_cell works with a known citation count; works in smaller cells fall back to larger baselines (see Details), and the result gains the columns n_cell and baseline.

    by_type

    Logical. If TRUE, baseline cells are also split by document type, normalised from works$type: articles and reviews get cells of their own and all other types get fnci = NA. Adds the column doc_type. Default FALSE.

    call

    Caller environment for error reporting.

    Value

    A tibble with one row per work and the columns work_id, field, year, cited_by_count, field_mean (the baseline: the mean citation count of the work's cell) and fnci. The column set depends on the arguments: by_type = TRUE adds doc_type ("article", "review" or NA), and min_cell adds n_cell (integer; the number of works with a known citation count in the baseline cell) and baseline (a factor with the levels field_year, field_year_pm1, year and none; the level the baseline comes from). An empty corpus gives a 0-row tibble with the same columns.

    Details

    FNCI is defined as:

    $$FNCI_i = \frac{C_i}{\bar{C}_{f,y}}$$

    Where \(C_i\) is the citation count of work i and \(\bar{C}_{f,y}\) is the mean citation count of all works in field f published in year y.

    An FNCI of 1.0 means the work is cited at the corpus average of its baseline cell (by default its field and year). Values > 1.0 indicate above-average impact.

    For "openalex_concepts", the highest-scoring level-0 concept from the concepts table is used. For "mesh", MeSH headings are used: concepts of the "mesh" vocabulary of sm_concept_vocabularies(), also when spelled "MEDLINE" (requires MeSH data in concepts; see below). For "manual", a field column must already exist in corpus$works.

    Small cells

    A cell with few works gives an unstable baseline, and a work alone in its cell gets FNCI = 1 by construction. When min_cell is NULL and more than 25% of the works with a citation count sit in cells with fewer than 10 such works, a message (class scimapR_fnci_small_cells) gives that share. sm_its() (outcome = "cnci") and sm_metric_summary() (metric = "cnci") show it too when they derive impact from citation counts.

    Fallback baselines

    With min_cell set, each work gets the most specific baseline that has at least min_cell works with a known citation count, the work itself included:

    1. field_year: its field and publication year;

    2. field_year_pm1: its field in the pooled years y - 1 to y + 1 (truncated at the edges of the corpus);

    3. year: all works of its publication year.

    If even the year has fewer than min_cell such works, fnci and field_mean are NA, baseline is "none" and n_cell gives the size of the year cell. Works without a field ("unclassified") start at the year level, and works without a year get NA throughout.

    In this mode field may list several categories separated by ;, as the Web of Science WC field does. A work belongs to the cell of each of its categories. For each category the most specific level that reaches min_cell is found, and the work's baseline is the average of the category baselines at the most specific level any of them reached: baseline names that level and n_cell is the smallest of the averaged cells. The baselines are averaged (\(C_i / mean(e_k)\)), not the ratios (\(mean(C_i / e_k)\)). field keeps the original string. Without min_cell the string is one field, as before.

    Document types

    With by_type = TRUE, works$type is normalised: lower-cased, its first ;-separated part, trimmed. "article" covers article, journal-article, jour and research-article; "review" covers review and review article. Works of any other or a missing type get fnci = NA (and baseline = NA), with one message (class scimapR_fnci_other_types). The type stays part of the cell at every fallback level. The PubMed and Semantic Scholar fetchers record every work as "journal-article", so their reviews count as articles.

    MeSH fields

    MeSH check tags (Humans, Animals, Male, Female, Pregnancy, the age groups, common laboratory and farm animals, and the historical periods) describe who or what was studied, and common descriptors of study design, statistics and laboratory material (such as Retrospective Studies, Risk Factors, Treatment Outcome or Cells, Cultured) describe how it was studied. Neither is ever used as a field.

    sm_fetch_pubmed(), sm_read_pubmed_xml() and sm_enrich_concepts() (source = "mesh") record each heading's major-topic flag as its score: 1 for a major topic of the article (starred in PubMed) and 0 otherwise. A work gets its highest-scoring heading; among several, the one that most works of the corpus carry (ties in alphabetical order). A work whose headings carry no scores, as with MeSH terms from other sources, gets its heading that is most frequent in the corpus, with one message (class scimapR_fnci_mesh_unscored). A work with no other headings is unclassified.

    References

    Waltman, L., van Eck, N. J., van Leeuwen, T. N., Visser, M. S., & van Raan, A. F. J. (2011). Towards a New Crown Indicator: Some Theoretical Considerations. Journal of Informetrics, 5(1), 37–47. doi:10.1016/j.joi.2010.08.001

    Examples

    corpus <- sm_example_corpus()
fnci <- sm_metric_fnci(corpus, classification = "openalex_concepts")
#> ℹ 100% of the works sit in field-year cells with fewer than 10 works, so their
#>   FNCI baselines rest on very few citation counts.
#> ℹ Set `min_cell` of `sm_metric_fnci()` to fall back to larger baselines for
#>   small cells.
head(fnci)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   work_id    field                    year cited_by_count field_mean  fnci
#>   <chr>      <chr>                   <int>          <int>      <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 W000000001 clinical outcomes        2023              3       10.2 0.293
#> 2 W000000002 colorectal cancer        2020              9       12.2 0.738
#> 3 W000000003 gene expression          2024             28       11.3 2.47 
#> 4 W000000004 spatial transcriptomics  2020             29       27.5 1.05 
#> 5 W000000005 immune checkpoint        2020             16       16   1    
#> 6 W000000006 immune checkpoint        2018             16       16   1    

# Fall back to larger baselines for cells with fewer than 5 works, with
# articles and reviews normalised separately
fnci <- sm_metric_fnci(corpus, min_cell = 5, by_type = TRUE)
#> ℹ 14 works of a type other than article or review get no FNCI with `by_type =
#>   TRUE`.
#> ℹ Type: "letter".
table(fnci$baseline, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>     field_year field_year_pm1           year           none           <NA> 
#>              5             34            132             15             14
